claim: Depression is among the leading causes of disability worldwide.
source: Depression is among the leading causes of disability worldwide, which reflects the current lack of understanding of its underlying mechanisms (Friedrich, 2017; Menke, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedrich, 2017 and Menke, 2018

claim: Metabolic alterations are emerging as key etiological factors for the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression.
source: Metabolic alterations are emerging as key etiological factors for the development of neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression (Pei and Wallace, 2018; Andreazza and Nierenberg, 2018; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pei and Wallace, 2018; Andreazza and Nierenberg, 2018; Kim et al., 2019

claim: The brain has strong reliance on high energy consumption.
source: The strong reliance of the brain on high energy consumption would make it particularly vulnerable to metabolic alterations (Pei and Wallace, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pei and Wallace, 2018

claim: Chronic stress has a strong capacity to trigger and exacerbate depression.
source: In addition, chronic stress has a strong capacity to trigger and exacerbate depression (de Kloet et al., 2005; Richter-Levin and Xu, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to de Kloet et al., 2005 and Richter-Levin and Xu, 2018

claim: Chronic stress impinges metabolic-costly neuronal adaptations in structure and function.
source: chronic stress has a strong capacity to trigger and exacerbate depression (de Kloet et al., 2005; Richter-Levin and Xu, 2018) and impinges metabolic-costly neuronal adaptations in structure and function (Turner and Lloyd, 2004; de Kloet et al., 2005; McEwen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Turner and Lloyd, 2004; de Kloet et al., 2005; McEwen et al., 2015

claim: Stress-associated depletion of brain's energy resources could lead to impaired neuronal plasticity underlying depression.
source: Accordingly, stress-associated depletion of brain's energy resources could lead to impaired neuronal plasticity underlying depression (Morava and Kozicz, 2013; Picard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morava and Kozicz, 2013 and Picard et al., 2018

claim: Mitochondria play a central role in the adaptation and response to stress by powering the brain with energy production.
source: Mitochondria, by powering the brain with energy production, play a central role in the adaptation and response to stress (Picard et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Picard et al., 2015

claim: Mitochondrial supplements could provide an efficient means of protecting brain structures that are particularly vulnerable to stress.
source: mitochondrial supplements could provide an efficient means of protecting brain structures that are particularly vulnerable to stress (Parikh et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parikh et al., 2009

claim: Not all individuals are equally affected by stress.
source: However, not all individuals are equally affected by stress (Duclot and Kabbaj, 2013; McEwen et al., 2015; Russo et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Duclot and Kabbaj, 2013; McEwen et al., 2015; Russo et al., 2012

claim: Some individuals show high vulnerability to develop depression while others endure resilience following stress exposure.
source: while some individuals show a high vulnerability to develop depression, others endure resilience following stress exposure (Russo et al., 2012; Weger and Sandi, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Russo et al., 2012 and Weger and Sandi, 2018

claim: High anxiety trait has great predictive power in defining stress vulnerability.
source: In addition to the great predictive power of high anxiety trait in defining stress vulnerability (Sandi et al., 2008; Castro et al., 2012; for reviews, see Sandi and Richter-Levin (2009); Russo et al., 2012; Weger and Sandi, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sandi et al., 2008; Castro et al., 2012; Sandi and Richter-Levin, 2009; Russo et al., 2012; Weger and Sandi, 2018

claim: Epidemiological, clinical and animal work point to a link between social hierarchies and depression.
source: epidemiological, clinical and animal work point to a link between social hierarchies and depression (Larrieu and Sandi, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larrieu and Sandi, 2018

claim: High rank C57BL/6J mice were more susceptible to display social avoidance following exposure to chronic social defeat stress than low rank mice.
source: Recently, in the C57BL/6J inbred mouse strain, we found that high rank animals were more susceptible to display social avoidance following exposure to chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), while low rank mice were not affected (Larrieu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larrieu et al., 2017

claim: 1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy is one of the few non-invasive methods that can provide direct information on brain metabolism in vivo.
source: Data from 1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy [1H-MRS; one of the few non-invasive methods that can provide direct information on brain metabolism in vivo (Duarte et al., 2012)]
evidence: Supported by citation to Duarte et al., 2012

claim: There is a relationship between the metabolic profile of the nucleus accumbens, social rank, and vulnerability to stress.
source: Data from 1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy [1H-MRS; one of the few non-invasive methods that can provide direct information on brain metabolism in vivo (Duarte et al., 2012)] revealed a relationship between the metabolic profile of the nucleus accumbens [NAc; a hub brain region for the regulation of motivated behaviors (Robbins and Everitt, 1996) implicated in the pathophysiology of depression (Francis and Lobo, 2017)], social rank, and vulnerability to stress.
evidence: Supported by citations to Duarte et al., 2012; Robbins and Everitt, 1996; Francis and Lobo, 2017

claim: The nucleus accumbens is a hub brain region for the regulation of motivated behaviors.
source: nucleus accumbens [NAc; a hub brain region for the regulation of motivated behaviors (Robbins and Everitt, 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Robbins and Everitt, 1996

claim: The nucleus accumbens is implicated in the pathophysiology of depression.
source: nucleus accumbens [NAc; a hub brain region for the regulation of motivated behaviors (Robbins and Everitt, 1996) implicated in the pathophysiology of depression (Francis and Lobo, 2017)]
evidence: Supported by citation to Francis and Lobo, 2017

claim: Under basal conditions, low rank mice showed lower levels of energy-related metabolites in the NAc than high rank mice.
source: Thus, while under basal conditions low rank showed lower levels of energy-related metabolites than high rank mice, it was only the low rank/resilient group that displayed increased metabolite levels following CSDS (Larrieu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larrieu et al., 2017

claim: Only the low rank/resilient group displayed increased metabolite levels in the NAc following chronic social defeat stress.
source: Thus, while under basal conditions low rank showed lower levels of energy-related metabolites than high rank mice, it was only the low rank/resilient group that displayed increased metabolite levels following CSDS (Larrieu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larrieu et al., 2017

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine has been shown to have promising potency to rapidly alleviate depressive-like symptoms in preclinical studies.
source: Acetyl-L-carnitine (LAC) has been recently shown to have promising potency to rapidly alleviate depressive-like symptoms in preclinical studies (Bigio et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Nasca et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bigio et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Nasca et al., 2013

claim: Emerging clinical evidence supports the good tolerability of acetyl-L-carnitine in humans.
source: and in humans, where emerging clinical evidence supports its good tolerability (Wang et al., 2014; Veronese et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2014 and Veronese et al., 2018

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine is an endogenous short-chain acetyl ester of free carnitine involved in the transport of long chain fatty acids into the mitochondria for degradation by beta oxidation.
source: LAC is an endogenous short-chain acetyl ester of free carnitine involved in the transport of long chain fatty acids into the mitochondria for degradation by beta oxidation thus, contributing to energy metabolism (Ferreira and McKenna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira and McKenna, 2017

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine can facilitate the removal of oxidative products.
source: In addition, LAC can facilitate the removal of oxidative products, provide acetyl groups for protein acetylation, be used as a precursor for acetylcholine, or be incorporated into neurotransmitters such as glutamate, glutamine and GABA (Ferreira and McKenna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira and McKenna, 2017

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine can provide acetyl groups for protein acetylation.
source: In addition, LAC can facilitate the removal of oxidative products, provide acetyl groups for protein acetylation, be used as a precursor for acetylcholine, or be incorporated into neurotransmitters such as glutamate, glutamine and GABA (Ferreira and McKenna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira and McKenna, 2017

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine can be used as a precursor for acetylcholine.
source: In addition, LAC can facilitate the removal of oxidative products, provide acetyl groups for protein acetylation, be used as a precursor for acetylcholine, or be incorporated into neurotransmitters such as glutamate, glutamine and GABA (Ferreira and McKenna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira and McKenna, 2017

claim: Acetyl-L-carnitine can be incorporated into neurotransmitters such as glutamate, glutamine and GABA.
source: In addition, LAC can facilitate the removal of oxidative products, provide acetyl groups for protein acetylation, be used as a precursor for acetylcholine, or be incorporated into neurotransmitters such as glutamate, glutamine and GABA (Ferreira and McKenna, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferreira and McKenna, 2017

claim: Lipid peroxidation has been shown to be increased by restraint stress in the striatum.
source: given that lipid peroxidation has been shown to be increased by restrain stress in the striatum (Atif et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Atif et al., 2008

claim: High rank mice (ranks 1 and 2) and low rank mice (ranks 3 and 4) displayed different time in the tube during the social confrontation tube test.
source: Specifically, we report here that high (ranks 1 and 2) and low (ranks 3 and 4) rank mice (Figure 1B and C; time in the tube 1–2 vs 1–4, p<0.001), displayed different profile for anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C with statistical significance p<0.001

claim: High rank mice spent more time in the open arms of an elevated plus maze compared to low rank mice.
source: It was reflected by a higher time spent in the open arms of an elevated plus maze (EPM) (Figure 1D; p<0.05)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: High rank mice showed an increased latency to enter the center of an open field compared to low rank mice.
source: as well as an increased latency to enter the center of an open field (OF) (Figure 1E, left; p<0.05) in high rank compared to low rank mice.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: High rank and low rank mice did not show differences in the percent time spent in the center of the open field.
source: However, the two groups did not show differences in the percent time spent in the center of the OF (Figure 1E, center), indicating that their difference in anxiety-like behaviors depends on the specific threat encountered.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E center panel

claim: No difference in locomotor activity was observed between high rank and low rank mice as measured by distance travelled in the open field.
source: Importantly, no difference in locomotor activity was observed, as the distance travelled by both groups in the OF was similar (Figure 1E, right; n.s.).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E right panel with no statistical significance

claim: High rank mice showed vulnerability to develop social avoidance after chronic restraint stress.
source: Strikingly, we revealed that the susceptibility to CSDS observed in high rank mice in our previous study (Larrieu et al., 2017) can be generalized to a non-social, chronic restraint stress (CRS) protocol. Indeed, high rank individuals were the ones that, after CRS, showed vulnerability to develop social avoidance towards an unfamiliar mouse in a social interaction test (SI) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Larrieu et al., 2017

claim: Low rank mice were not affected by chronic restraint stress in terms of social avoidance.
source: In contrast, low rank mice seemed not being affected by stress exposure (social avoidance score: interaction, F1,21=7.75, p<0.05; time in interaction zone: interaction, F1,21=12.80, p<0.005).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing interaction effects

claim: Chronic restraint stress led to a significant decrease in cumulative body weight gain in high rank mice.
source: Animals exposed to CRS displayed a significant decrease in cumulative body weight gain, regardless of their social rank, that was not counteracted by LAC supplementation (Figure 2B; in high rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 45.0, p<0.0001 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; in low rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 20.4, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance p<0.0001

claim: Chronic restraint stress led to a significant decrease in cumulative body weight gain in low rank mice.
source: Animals exposed to CRS displayed a significant decrease in cumulative body weight gain, regardless of their social rank, that was not counteracted by LAC supplementation (Figure 2B; in high rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 45.0, p<0.0001 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; in low rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 20.4, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance p<0.001

claim: LAC supplementation did not counteract the stress-induced decrease in cumulative body weight gain.
source: Animals exposed to CRS displayed a significant decrease in cumulative body weight gain, regardless of their social rank, that was not counteracted by LAC supplementation (Figure 2B; in high rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 45.0, p<0.0001 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; in low rank: Stress effect F2,10 = 20.4, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Stress led to an increase in liquid consumption (+15 ± 12%) in the stressed groups.
source: Importantly, whereas stress led to an increase in liquid consumption (+15 ± 12%) in the stressed groups (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: There was no difference in liquid consumption between the CRS and CRS + LAC groups.
source: there was no difference in liquid consumption between the CRS and CRS + LAC groups (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: LAC treatment did not prevent the increase in social avoidance induced by chronic restraint stress in high rank mice.
source: We found that LAC treatment did not prevent the increase in social avoidance induced CRS in a group of 6 high rank mice (Figure 2D; n.s.).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D with no statistical significance

claim: LAC treatment abolished the chronic restraint stress-induced increase in passive coping behaviors in high rank mice in the forced swim test.
source: Indeed, LAC treatment was effective to abolish CRS-induced increase in passive coping behaviors in high rank mice in the FST (Figure 2E). Specifically, a significant increase in the immobility time observed in high rank mice following CRS exposure (Figure 2E; F2,15=5.31, p<0.05), was prevented by LAC supplementation (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Chronic restraint stress led to increased depressive-like behaviors in high rank mice as measured by a composite behavioral score.
source: ANOVA of these data indicated a significant effect of treatments (Figure 2F; F2,15=10.31, p<0.005); specifically, CRS led to increased depressive-like behaviors (p<0.005) that was restored by LAC (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance p<0.005

claim: LAC treatment restored the chronic restraint stress-induced increase in depressive-like behaviors in high rank mice as measured by a composite behavioral score.
source: ANOVA of these data indicated a significant effect of treatments (Figure 2F; F2,15=10.31, p<0.005); specifically, CRS led to increased depressive-like behaviors (p<0.005) that was restored by LAC (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: The 1H-MRS acquisitions led to a spectral signal-to-noise ratio of 17.5 ± 0.3 with a linewidth of 16 ± 1 Hz.
source: Our 1H-MRS acquisitions led to a spectral signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 17.5 ± 0.3 with a linewidth of 16 ± 1 Hz after shimming with FAST(EST)MAP.
evidence: Directly reported measurement from the study

claim: The acquired NAc spectra allowed quantification of up to 20 metabolites with LCModel.
source: The acquired NAc spectra allowed us to quantify up to 20 metabolites with LCModel (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: Factor analysis revealed three main factors that accounted for 31%, 12% and 9% of total variance.
source: First, we applied an unbiased multivariate factor analysis (FA) that revealed three main factors that accounted for 31%, 12% and 9% of total variance (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: Factor one included metabolites taurine, glutamate, phosphocreatine, N-acetylaspartate, γ-aminobutyric acid, creatine, myo-inositol, aspartate, phosphocholine, glucose, glutathione and ascorbate with loadings above 0.4.
source: Individual metabolites with loadings above 0.4 in Factor one included taurine (Tau), glutamate (Glu), phosphocreatine (PCr), N-acetylaspartate (NAA), γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), creatine (Cr), myo-inositol (Ins), aspartate (Asp), phosphocholine (PCho), glucose (Glc), glutathione (GSH) and ascorbate (Asc) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5

claim: Factor two included metabolites phosphocholine, glycerophosphorylcholine, and ascorbate with loadings above 0.4.
source: Metabolites with loading above 0.4 for the two other components were PCho, glycerophosphorylcholine (GPC), and Asc for Factor two
evidence: Reported from factor analysis results

claim: Factor three included metabolites glutamine and lactate with loadings above 0.4.
source: Metabolites with loading above 0.4 for the two other components were PCho, glycerophosphorylcholine (GPC), and Asc for Factor two, and glutamine (Gln) and lactate (Lac) for Factor three (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6

claim: Only Factor one was able to discriminate for stress and treatment response between high rank/vulnerable mice.
source: Only Factor one was able to discriminate for stress and treatment response between high rank/vulnerable mice (Figure 4B; F2,13=7.04; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance p<0.01

claim: In high rank mice, chronic restraint stress led to a reduction in Factor one metabolites compared to non-stressed high rank mice.
source: Specifically, in high rank mice, CRS led to a reduction in factor one metabolites as compared to their non-stressed high rank counterparts (p<0.005).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p<0.005

claim: LAC treatment reversed the effect of chronic restraint stress on Factor one metabolic profile in high rank mice.
source: Importantly, LAC treatment reversed the effect of CRS on Factor one metabolic profile (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p<0.05

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the behavioral composite z-score for depressive-like behaviors and Factor one metabolite levels in high rank mice.
source: Interestingly, we further found a significant negative correlation between the behavioral composite z-score for depressive-like behaviors in high rank mice and their Factor one metabolite levels (Figure 4C; R = −0.58, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C with correlation coefficient R = −0.58 and p<0.05

claim: The stress effect in Factor one was mainly carried by changes in taurine, phosphocreatine, glutamate, aspartate and N-acetyl-aspartate.
source: In metabolites strongly loading in factor one, we found that the observed stress effect was mainly carried by changes in Tau (p<0.05), PCr (p<0.05), Glu (p<0.05), Asp (p<0.05) and NAA (p<0.05), while the stress-reversing effects of LAC were driven by Tau (p<0.05) and PCr (p<0.05) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5 with statistical significance p<0.05 for each metabolite

claim: The stress-reversing effects of LAC were driven by taurine and phosphocreatine.
source: In metabolites strongly loading in factor one, we found that the observed stress effect was mainly carried by changes in Tau (p<0.05), PCr (p<0.05), Glu (p<0.05), Asp (p<0.05) and NAA (p<0.05), while the stress-reversing effects of LAC were driven by Tau (p<0.05) and PCr (p<0.05) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5 with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: Glutamine and phosphocholine were reduced by chronic restraint stress and reversed by LAC treatment.
source: Among the rest of metabolites that either loaded below 0.5 in Factor one or loaded in the other two factors (Figure 6A), we found that Gln and PCho were similarly reduced by CRS (p<0.05) and reversed by LAC treatment (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: The ratio of GPC over PCho was reduced by LAC treatment.
source: Notably, the ratio of GPC over PCho, that is the level of degradation product of phospholipids over their precursor, respectively, was reduced by LAC (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p<0.05

claim: There is a negative correlation between immobility time in the forced swim test and taurine levels.
source: In further correlational analyses addressed to identify potentially relevant treatment targets, we found two negative correlations, one between immobility time in the FST and taurine levels (R = −0.52, p<0.05)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with R = −0.52 and p<0.05

claim: There is a negative correlation between the composite behavioral z-score and GABA levels.
source: In further correlational analyses addressed to identify potentially relevant treatment targets, we found two negative correlations, one between immobility time in the FST and taurine levels (R = −0.52, p<0.05) and a second one between the composite behavioral z-score and GABA (R = −0.55, p<0.05) (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B-D with correlation coefficient R = −0.55 and p<0.05

claim: Social rank in mice predicts vulnerability to stress.
source: Our results reinforce the view that social rank in mice predicts vulnerability to stress.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings on high rank mice showing vulnerability to stress

claim: The vulnerability of high rank mice to stress is not solely based upon loss of social status.
source: In addition, given the non-social character of the CRS protocol, our results argue against the view that their vulnerability would be solely based upon loss of social status (Larrieu and Sandi, 2018).
evidence: Inferred from the use of non-social chronic restraint stress showing similar vulnerability in high rank mice, with citation to Larrieu and Sandi, 2018

claim: Under basal conditions, higher rank is related to higher anxiety-like behaviors as indicated by exploration of an elevated plus maze.
source: It is important to note that, under basal conditions (i.e., before stress application), higher rank is related to higher anxiety-like behaviors as indicated by their exploration of an elevated plus maze
evidence: Supported by data from the study showing high rank mice spent more time in open arms of EPM

claim: High anxiety trait is a well-established risk factor to develop stress-related depressive behaviors.
source: as high anxiety trait is a well-established risk factor to develop stress-related depressive behaviors (Sandi et al., 2008; Castro et al., 2012; for reviews, see Sandi and Richter-Levin (2009); Russo et al., 2012; Weger and Sandi, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sandi et al., 2008; Castro et al., 2012; Sandi and Richter-Levin, 2009; Russo et al., 2012; Weger and Sandi, 2018

claim: LAC levels are markedly reduced in patients with major depressive disorder.

claim: LAC treatment reduces immobility time in the forced swim test in rodents.
source: Our results in the FST are in line with previous rodent studies showing the ability of LAC to reduce immobility time in this test (Wang et al., 2015; Bigio et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2017; Pulvirenti et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015; Bigio et al., 2016; Lau et al., 2017; Pulvirenti et al., 1990

claim: Several small clinical trials in humans report effectiveness of LAC treatment in amelioration of depressive symptoms.
source: with several small clinical trials in humans reporting effectiveness of LAC treatment in amelioration of depressive symptoms (Martinotti et al., 2011; Pettegrew et al., 2002; Zanardi and Smeraldi, 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Pettegrew et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martinotti et al., 2011; Pettegrew et al., 2002; Zanardi and Smeraldi, 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Pettegrew et al., 2000

claim: LAC can ameliorate both social interaction and social avoidance at the chronic restraint stress and social defeat stress paradigms in mice with baseline anxiety-like behavior, increased systemic inflammation and decreased hippocampal volume.
source: Growing evidence showed the ability of LAC to ameliorate both social interaction and social avoidance at the chronic restraint stress and social defeat stress paradigms in mice with baseline anxiety-like behavior, increased systemic inflammation and decreased hippocampal volume (Lau et al., 2017; Nasca et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lau et al., 2017 and Nasca et al., 2019

claim: Pharmacological manipulations leading to either impaired or boosted mitochondrial function in the nucleus accumbens were found to affect energetically-costly high rank behaviors during a social competition test between two male rats.
source: This postulate is supported by previous studies that showed that pharmacological manipulations leading to either impaired or boosted mitochondrial function in the nucleus accumbens were found to boost energetically-costly high rank behaviors during a social competition test between two male rats (Hollis et al., 2015; van der Kooij et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hollis et al., 2015 and van der Kooij et al., 2018a

claim: Active coping in the forced swim test depends upon dopamine actions in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Active coping in the FST depends upon dopamine actions in the NAc (Tye et al., 2013; de Kloet and Molendijk, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tye et al., 2013 and de Kloet and Molendijk, 2016

claim: LAC increases dopamine release in vivo.
source: and LAC has been shown to increase DA release in vivo (Harsing et al., 1992; Tolu et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Harsing et al., 1992 and Tolu et al., 2002

claim: LAC prevents a chronic stress-induced decrease in dopamine output in the nucleus accumbens shell.
source: and to prevent a chronic stress-induced decrease in DA output in the NAc shell (Masi et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Masi et al., 2003

claim: Stress induces alterations in the accumbal oxidative stress system.
source: In addition, stress has been shown to induce alterations in the accumbal oxidative stress system (Della et al., 2012; Ignácio et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Della et al., 2012 and Ignácio et al., 2017

claim: LAC treatment exerts neuroprotective effects by inhibition of glial activation and oxidative stress in the striatum in an animal model of dopaminergic neuron damage.
source: and LAC treatment to exert neuroprotective effects by inhibition of glial activation and oxidative stress in the striatum in an animal model of DAergic neuron damage (Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2016

claim: Lipid peroxidation is increased by immobilization stress in the rat striatum.
source: Furthermore, lipid peroxidation has been shown to be increased by immobilization stress in the rat striatum and L-carnitine to reduce associated striatal lipid peroxidation (Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011

claim: L-carnitine reduces striatal lipid peroxidation associated with immobilization stress.
source: Furthermore, lipid peroxidation has been shown to be increased by immobilization stress in the rat striatum and L-carnitine to reduce associated striatal lipid peroxidation (Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011

claim: LAC was effective to reverse lipid peroxidation damage in stressed rodents while being devoid of effect in controls.
source: Interestingly, both in rodents (Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011) and in zebrafish (Marcon et al., 2019), LAC was effective to reverse lipid peroxidation damage in stressed animals while being devoid of effect in controls.
evidence: Supported by citations to Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011 and Marcon et al., 2019

claim: LAC was effective to reverse lipid peroxidation damage in stressed zebrafish while being devoid of effect in controls.
source: Interestingly, both in rodents (Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011) and in zebrafish (Marcon et al., 2019), LAC was effective to reverse lipid peroxidation damage in stressed animals while being devoid of effect in controls.
evidence: Supported by citations to Méndez-Cuesta et al., 2011 and Marcon et al., 2019

claim: Taurine is a sulfur containing amino acid with no involvement in protein synthesis.
source: Taurine is a sulfur containing amino acid, with no involvement in protein synthesis, but with several functions ranging from antioxidant, signaling molecule and osmolyte (Hansen et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Jamshidzadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Jamshidzadeh et al., 2017

claim: Taurine has several functions including antioxidant, signaling molecule and osmolyte.
source: Taurine is a sulfur containing amino acid, with no involvement in protein synthesis, but with several functions ranging from antioxidant, signaling molecule and osmolyte (Hansen et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Jamshidzadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016; Jamshidzadeh et al., 2017

claim: Brain taurine concentrations are reduced by chronic stress.

claim: Brain taurine concentrations are reduced by hyperglycemic conditions.

claim: LAC reverses ageing-induced reductions in taurine specifically in the striatum.
source: Strikingly, in an early study, Sershen et al. (1991) specifically observed a reversal by LAC of ageing-induced reductions in taurine in the striatum, not of any other amino acid in the striatum or of taurine or other amino acids in any other brain region.
